title: Short-Circuit Evaluation
summary: Understand how && and || optimize execution by skipping unnecessary right-hand expressions, and learn to write safe guard patterns.
learningObjectives: Understand why and how Java short-circuits && and || operators
Use short-circuiting to build safe guard conditions against division by zero and null pointers
Identify bugs caused by side-effects (like increment) inside short-circuited expressions
Differentiate between short-circuit (&&, ||) and non-short-circuit (&, |) operators
expectedOutcomes: Write crash-proof conditional guards in enterprise Java code
Confidently answer technical interview questions regarding short-circuit evaluation

activities.title: Smart Evaluation with Short-Circuiting

breakdown.whatIsIt: Short-circuit evaluation skips evaluating the second condition in && (if the first is false) or in || (if the first is true).
breakdown.whyItMatters: It prevents runtime crashes (like dividing by zero or NullPointerExceptions) and improves performance.
howItWorks: Evaluates strictly from left to right.
keyTakeaways: Use short-circuiting to build safe guard conditions on the left.
Never put side-effects like count++ inside logical conditions.
Use && and ||, not single & and | for boolean logic.

questions.question: In the expression (false && rightExpression), will rightExpression be evaluated?
questions.explanation: Because the left operand is false, the result of && must be false regardless. Java skips rightExpression.
hints: false AND anything is always false.

questions.prompt: In the expression (true || rightExpression), will rightExpression be evaluated?
questions.question: In the expression (true || rightExpression), will rightExpression be evaluated?
questions.explanation: Because the left operand is true, the result of || must be true regardless. Java skips rightExpression.
hints: true OR anything is always true.

questions.prompt: What is the value of count after: int count = 5; boolean b = (10 > 2) || (++count > 0); ?
questions.question: What is the value of count after: int count = 5; boolean b = (10 > 2) || (++count > 0); ?
questions.explanation: Because (10 > 2) is true, the || operator short-circuits. ++count is NEVER executed, leaving count at 5.
hints: The left side of || is true, so the right side is skipped.

questions.prompt: What happens when running: int denom = 0; if (denom != 0 & 10 / denom > 1) {} (note single &)?
questions.question: What happens when running: int denom = 0; if (denom != 0 & 10 / denom > 1) {} (note single &)?
options: It compiles with a warning and prints false
questions.explanation: Single & is a non-short-circuiting operator. It evaluates both sides unconditionally. When evaluating 10 / denom, it crashes with an ArithmeticException.

questions.prompt: What is the primary benefit of short-circuit evaluation in enterprise applications?
questions.question: What is the primary benefit of short-circuit evaluation in enterprise applications?
options: It avoids unnecessary expensive method calls and prevents null/zero runtime crashes
It makes code run in parallel threads
It replaces the need for loops
questions.explanation: Short-circuiting avoids executing expensive secondary operations and allows writing safe guards (like checking non-null or non-zero).
hints: Think about performance and avoiding crashes.

activities.title: Top Placement Interview Questions: Short-Circuit Evaluation

interviewQA.question: Explain short-circuit evaluation in Java with an example.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Short-circuit evaluation is a language optimization where the second operand in a logical expression (`&&` or `||`) is only evaluated if the first operand does not definitively determine the result. For example, in `(x != 0 && y / x > 2)`, if `x` is `0`, `x != 0` is `false`. Since `false && anything` is always `false`, Java skips `y / x`, safely preventing an `ArithmeticException: / by zero`.
keyPoints: && skips if left is false; || skips if left is true; used to guard against crashes.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between '&&' and '&' when used with boolean operands?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `&&` is a short-circuit operator: if the left operand is `false`, the right operand is skipped. `&` is a logical (bitwise) operator that does NOT short-circuit: it forces evaluation of both operands regardless of the left operand's value.

interviewQA.question: Why is it considered dangerous to use increment or decrement operators inside boolean conditions?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Because short-circuiting can cause the increment/decrement to be skipped conditionally. For instance, in `if (flag && count++ > 0)`, `count` is only incremented when `flag` is `true`. If `flag` is `false`, `count` is unchanged, leading to erratic state and intermittent bugs.
keyPoints: Side-effects in short-circuited expressions may execute intermittently, causing subtle bugs.

interviewQA.question: How does short-circuit evaluation help prevent NullPointerExceptions in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: You can guard an object method call by checking if the reference is non-null first: `if (user != null && user.isActive())`. If `user` is `null`, the left condition evaluates to `false`, and Java short-circuits, never calling `.isActive()` on a null reference.
keyPoints: Guards like (obj != null && obj.method()) safely prevent NullPointerExceptions.

interviewQA.question: What will be printed by: int a = 1; if (a < 0 && a++ > 0) {} System.out.println(a);?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: It will print `1`. Because `a < 0` (`1 < 0`) is `false`, the `&&` operator short-circuits immediately. The second operand `a++ > 0` is never evaluated, so `a` remains `1`.
keyPoints: Left false skips right operand, preserving a at 1.

activities.title: Topic Confidence Checklist
checklist: I know that false && skips the second condition.
I know that true || skips the second condition.
I can write safe guards to prevent division by zero.
I never put mutating operations (like ++) inside logical conditions.
I understand the difference between && and single &.
